ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening against the OFAC Consolidated Sanctions List, Global Affairs Canada Canadian Sanctions List (under SEMA and the United Nations Act), United Nations Security Council consolidated list, and the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act registrant list; mandatory domestic and foreign PEP classification and risk-rating under PCMLTFA ss 9.2-9.5; verification of Criminal Code corruption records; enhanced due diligence on all virtual-brand franchisor counterparties, delivery-platform payout beneficiaries (UberEats, DoorDash), and ghost-kitchen subtenants; FINTRAC client identification and record-keeping for food-delivery MSB payment rails.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Inc incorporating service administered by the Corporate Registry, Service Alberta, with NUANS name search executed through accredited corporate registry service providers under the Alberta Business Corporations Act corporate naming regime)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must be English or French transliterated into Latin script; a name must contain a distinctive element, a descriptive element, and a legal element (Unlimited, ULC, Corporation, Inc., Corp., Ltd.); numeric-designated incorporations are available where no name approval can be obtained; use of 'Alberta' requires provincial consent and use of 'Canada' requires Global Affairs Canada consent; non-Latin brand elements must be rendered in Latin script for the registered corporate name while a corresponding unregistered trade/style name may retain native script.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon official rejection, the applicant must file a written Request for Reconsideration to the Director of the Corporate Registry, Service Alberta, within 30 days of the rejection notice; the submission must include the preserved or freshly ordered NUANS search report, letters of consent from any previously distinct or registered entities, and a redrafted distinctive-element proposal; if reconsideration is denied, the applicant may file a new name approval application or proceed with a numeric-designated incorporation and thereafter register a trade/style name; no administrative filing fee is refundable upon rejection.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual registered office is permissible in Alberta for a ULC engaged in ghost-kitchen and virtual-brand operations, provided the registered office is a physical address within Alberta at which process can be served and statutory records are maintained; the delivery-only food production facility must hold a separate licensed commercial food premises registration with Alberta Health Services (AHS) or CFIA, and the licensed kitchen address cannot be replaced by the virtual corporate office.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Medium-High for licensed food premises: unannounced Alberta Health Services and municipal food-safety inspections occur with approximately 30-60% probability in the first 12 months of operation for delivery-only kitchen facilities; Low (<10%) for the corporate registered office absent an enforcement file, regulatory complaint, or investigative trigger related to AML/CFT or beneficial ownership verification.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, including sections 5-7 (incorporation and articles), 102-105 (directors), 106 (officers), and 119 (registered office). Confirm the ULC designation and unlimited-liability provisions with Alberta Corporate Registry before filing; Alberta corporate law and tax treatment are distinct from British Columbia ULC rules.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction, through an authorized Alberta registry agent.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 1 under the Alberta Business Corporations Regulation), submitted with the required Notice of Address and Notice of Directors.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital or incorporation escrow account is generally required. Shares may be issued for consideration determined by the directors, subject to the Act and the articles. The stated USD filing fee is an approximate conversion of the Alberta government incorporation fee of CAD 275; registry-agent charges and exchange rates vary.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that the Corporation accept the subscriptions for the shares set out in the subscription agreements and issue those shares upon receipt of the applicable consideration, with entries made in the securities register. RESOLVED that the registered office and records office be established at the Alberta addresses approved by the directors and maintained in the Corporation’s records. RESOLVED that [Name] be appointed President and [Name] Secretary, each to serve until resignation or replacement by the directors. RESOLVED that each officer is authorized to complete routine incorporation, tax, banking, licensing, and registration filings, subject to the Act and further board approval where required.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Confirm ULC eligibility and reserve the corporate name
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry through an authorized Alberta registry agent; NUANS name-search system where a named corporation is proposed.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Confirm with the registry agent that the proposed entity can be incorporated in Alberta with the intended unlimited-liability designation and that its articles will record that status. Obtain an Alberta NUANS report for a named corporation and file within the report's validity period; alternatively use an eligible numbered name. A name reservation or NUANS report does not itself incorporate the corporation.
required_dossiers: Proposed legal name or numbered-name instruction
Alberta NUANS report if using a named corporation
Proposed registered-office and records-office addresses in Alberta
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected or conflicts with an existing name or trademark, amend the name or use a numbered name and resubmit. Obtain separate trademark advice; registry name approval does not establish trademark rights.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: File incorporation documents and statutory notices
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction, via an authorized Alberta registry agent.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Execute and submit Articles of Incorporation (Form 1), Notice of Address, and Notice of Directors through the registry agent. State the share structure, restrictions, and any required ULC designation accurately. Provide the incorporator's prescribed declarations and pay the government fee and agent service charges. Foreign-executed documents should be signed in the form accepted by the agent; notarization, authentication, or certified translation may be requested for foreign identity or authority documents but is not a universal requirement for standard Alberta incorporation.
required_dossiers: Identification and authority documents requested by the registry agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: For a rejected or queried filing, obtain the registry agent's deficiency notice, correct the articles or notices, provide supporting evidence, and resubmit. Do not represent the entity as incorporated until the Certificate of Incorporation is issued.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organize corporate records and adopt initial governance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: The corporation's directors and Alberta registered office; Alberta Corporate Registry for any required subsequent statutory notices.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After issuance of the certificate, hold the organizational board meeting or execute written directors' resolutions. Approve subscriptions and share issuances, appoint officers, adopt the registered office, authorize banking and tax registrations, and establish the corporate records and securities registers. Record individuals with significant control as required by the Act, maintain the register, and file any required updates with the registry. Obtain signed shareholder consents or resolutions where required.
required_dossiers: Certificate and filed Articles of Incorporation
Share subscription agreements and evidence of consideration
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Correct incomplete corporate records by passing valid confirmatory resolutions and updating registers. File overdue statutory notices promptly and obtain legal advice before ratifying acts that may exceed directors' authority.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Complete tax, employer, and municipal business registrations
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency Business Registration Online; applicable Alberta and municipal authorities.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Obtain a CRA business number and register the required program accounts, including GST/HST and payroll where applicable. Confirm the corporation's tax classification and cross-border consequences of unlimited liability with Canadian and relevant foreign tax advisers; ULC tax treatment is not automatically pass-through for Canadian purposes. Apply for the municipal business licence and zoning approval for the kitchen premises before operations.
required_dossiers: GST/HST and payroll account information, if applicable
Municipal licence and land-use application materials
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Resolve CRA identity or account-verification issues through CRA's business enquiries channel and provide corporate records. For municipal zoning or licence objections, seek written reasons, amend the use or premises plan, and use the municipality's reconsideration or appeal procedure.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Alberta Health Services Environmental Public Health for food-establishment review and food-handling permits; the municipality for business licensing, land use, building, plumbing, and development approvals. Alberta has no general provincial industrial licensing board for ordinary ghost-kitchen operations.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Alberta Health Services Food Handling Permit (where required for the proposed food establishment), together with the applicable municipal business licence and development/building approvals.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: A delivery-only commercial kitchen is not ordinarily a designated project requiring a full environmental impact assessment under Alberta's Environmental Assessment (Mandatory and Exempted Activities) Regulation. Confirm project-specific screening with the agency if the facility includes a separately regulated activity, significant emissions, or a designated-project trigger.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No single ghost-kitchen-specific numerical wastewater or VOC threshold applies. Discharge must comply with the municipality's sewer-use bylaw and applicable provincial approvals; fats, oils, and grease must be controlled as required by the local authority. Manage solid waste, used cooking oil, and hazardous materials under applicable provincial and municipal rules. Install and operate grease interception and exhaust controls as required by plumbing, fire, building, and municipal codes.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Obtain applicable development and building permits, occupancy approval, plumbing and gas approvals, and fire inspection or fire-safety approval from the municipal authority or fire service. Verify ventilation, commercial cooking suppression, exits, occupant loads, and structural capacity. Comply with Alberta Occupational Health and Safety legislation, including hazard assessment, worker training, first aid, and workplace requirements. Alberta does not issue a single general workplace-clearance certificate for all kitchens.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC). Online portals: Business Registration Online (BRO), My Business Account (MyBA), and GST/HST NETFILE for electronic return filing. The CRA administers federal corporate income tax, GST/HST, and collects Alberta corporate income tax on behalf of the Province of Alberta under the federal-provincial tax collection agreement.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1 - Incorporate the ULC under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta) and obtain the Certificate of Incorporation from the Alberta Corporate Registry (the ULC is a separate statutory corporation available to non-resident owners). Step 2 - Register with the CRA for the 9-digit Business Number (BN), which is the universal Canadian tax identifier; apply online via BRO for same-day issuance or file Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number and Certain Program Accounts) with the CRA tax centre, processing in 2 to 6 weeks. Step 3 - Activate program accounts: (i) RC account for T2 corporate income tax; the account is normally auto-created upon incorporation and the T2 return is due within 6 months of each taxation year-end; (ii) RT account for GST/HST, mandatory once the CAD 30,000 small-supplier threshold is exceeded, with non-resident applicants using Form GST494-1; (iii) RP account for payroll where the ghost-kitchen operator employs Canadian staff, triggering source deduction remittances. Step 4 - The CRA issues a BN confirmation letter; registration is effective on the date the BN is assigned or as specified in the account application. Step 5 - If the ULC is controlled by non-residents, dividends paid to non-resident shareholders are subject to Part XIII non-resident withholding tax (statutory 25%, often treaty-reduced) and the ULC must file NR4 information returns; no separate Alberta tax identification number is needed because Alberta corporate tax is collected by the CRA under the collection agreement.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible (U.S. federal check-the-box via Form 8832 and transitional Alberta ULC flow-through election under the Revenue Amendment Act, 2021) / Entity_Level_Taxation (Canadian federal and provincial statutory default). For Canadian income tax purposes the Alberta ULC is a corporation under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and a 'taxable corporation' under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. It files as a separate taxpayer on its worldwide income if central management and control is situated in Canada. Combined general corporate rate in Alberta: 15% federal plus 8% provincial = 23%; the reduced 11% small-business rate (9% federal plus 2% provincial) is unavailable where more than 50% of the shares are owned by non-residents because the ULC would not qualify as a Canadian-controlled private corporation.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: (i) U.S. Form 8832 check-the-box election: permits the ULC to be classified as a disregarded entity or partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes only; it has no effect on Canadian entity classification. (ii) Alberta transitional ULC election: pre-existing ULCs may elect under the Revenue Amendment Act 2021 to retain member-level flow-through treatment for Alberta income tax for a transitional period, while newly incorporated ULCs are taxed at the entity level. (iii) GST/HST closely related corporation election under section 156 of the Excise Tax Act: the ULC and its 90%-or-more owned subsidiaries may elect to be treated as a single registrant, simplifying intercompany GST/HST accounting. (iv) Voluntary GST/HST registration election under subsection 240(3) of the Excise Tax Act: a small supplier may elect early registration to recover input tax credits.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Value Added Tax - Goods and Services Tax (GST) / Harmonized Sales Tax (HST). Alberta does not participate in the HST and imposes no provincial retail sales tax, therefore the operative indirect tax in Alberta is the 5% federal GST.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) made by the entity in the immediately preceding four consecutive calendar quarters or in any single calendar quarter; the threshold is aggregated with taxable supplies of associated persons under section 148 of the Excise Tax Act. A multi-brand ghost kitchen must aggregate revenue from all virtual brands. Registration becomes mandatory once the CAD 30,000 threshold is exceeded; failure to register attracts a penalty equal to the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the net tax not collected.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no statutory real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory API stamping, or digital stamping regime. GST/HST registrants must issue invoices, in paper or electronic form, containing the particulars set out in section 3 of Schedule V to the GST/HST Regulations: supplier name, Business Number, date of invoice, description of goods or services, and tax amount. Electronic records and invoices must be maintained in a CRA-readable format for six years under section 286 of the Excise Tax Act. Registrants with annual taxable supplies exceeding CAD 1 million must file GST/HST returns electronically via GST/HST NETFILE. The CRA is developing a voluntary Pan-Canadian E-Invoicing framework based on the PEPPOL standard; deployment remains optional and there is no clearance mandate. Digital platform operators such as DoorDash and UberEats are separately subject to the Information Return for Digital Platform Operators (effective 1 January 2023), which imposes due-diligence and seller-reporting duties unrelated to e-invoicing.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating at 0% GST/HST is available for supplies of goods exported directly by the supplier under section 6 of Part V, Schedule VI of the Excise Tax Act, including prepared foods and co-packed virtual-brand products shipped by the operator or its carrier to a destination outside Canada. Supplies of services to a non-resident purchaser are zero-rated under section 7 of Part V, Schedule VI where the services are performed entirely outside Canada, or are performed partly in Canada but relate to real property situated outside Canada or to goods outside Canada and are for consumption outside Canada, and the purchaser is not registered under Part IX and carries on no business in Canada; this covers virtual-brand licensing fees and management or technology fees charged to a foreign parent. Domestic ghost-kitchen sales to Canadian consumers through DoorDash or UberEats are taxable at 5% GST. Export eligibility requires direct export with no intermediate Canadian processing or sale, contemporaneous proof of physical export movement, and retention of supporting records for six years.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration - Form B13A Goods to be Exported filed through the Canadian Automated Export Declaration (CAED) system or the carrier's cargo report for shipments above CAD 2,000, including the assigned Export Report Number
Transport evidence - Bill of Lading (ocean), Air Waybill, truck manifest, or courier shipment scan history showing delivery to an address outside Canada
Commercial Invoice and Purchase Order or Sales Contract describing the exported goods, quantity, price, and foreign destination
Inward Remittance Certificate - bank-issued proof of foreign currency receipt, SWIFT MT103 credit advice, or bank statement evidencing settlement of the export consideration
Cargo control or customs broker documentation demonstrating border exit and foreign customs entry
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA's normal reassessment period for a corporation is four years from the date of the original notice of assessment under section 298 of the Excise Tax Act; the limitation period is unlimited where misrepresentation, neglect, or wilful default is proven. Where export zero-rating is claimed without eligible documentation, the supply is reassessed as taxable at 5% GST, any related input tax credits are clawed back, and compound daily interest accrues at prescribed CRA rates. Gross-negligence penalties equal the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the net tax sought to be avoided under subsection 280(1) of the Excise Tax Act. Criminal evasion under section 327 is punishable on summary conviction by a fine of up to 200% of the evaded tax and/or 2 years imprisonment, and on indictment by a fine of up to 250% and/or 5 years imprisonment. Directors of the ULC are jointly and severally liable for unremitted GST/HST under subsection 323(1) unless they exercised the standard of care of a reasonably prudent person. The Excise Tax Act prescribes no statutory F/X repatriation deadline; the 180-day benchmark is a documentary best-practice standard, and prolonged non-receipt of export proceeds will trigger audit scrutiny and retrospective clawback of zero-rating benefits.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada, with prudential banking oversight by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), anti-money-laundering supervision by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), and no dedicated foreign-exchange-control authority; Canada does not maintain a centralized exchange-approval regime.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada observes full Article VIII convertibility for both current-account and capital-account transactions. The Canadian dollar is freely floating and fully convertible. There are no prior-exchange-control licenses, no non-resident remittance permits, and no restriction on inbound equity investment into an Alberta unlimited liability corporation. Practical hurdles to profit remittance are corporate solvency under the Alberta Business Corporations Act and Canadian withholding tax under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act. Dividends paid by the ULC to a non-resident shareholder are subject to the statutory 25% withholding rate unless reduced under an applicable tax treaty; the Canada-U.S. treaty may reduce this rate to 5% or 15%, depending on shareholding and treaty eligibility. A ULC may distribute funds only if the solvency test is satisfied and directors have approved the remittance.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory surrender rule, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no timeline for converting export receipts in Canada. Exporters may retain foreign currency balances in Canadian or offshore accounts, may convert freely, and may use such balances for foreign operating expenses. For regulatory reporting, cross-border electronic funds transfers of CAD 10,000 or more are reportable to FINTRAC by the transmitting financial institution. If the ULC holds specified foreign property, including foreign bank or investment accounts, with an aggregate cost amount exceeding CAD 100,000, Form T1135 must be filed with the Canada Revenue Agency. Export proceeds recognized in Canadian taxable income are converted into Canadian dollars using the Bank of Canada annual average exchange rate or the CRA exchange rate for the relevant taxation year.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-Medium. Offshore electronic money institutions are not recognized as Schedule I banks under the Bank Act and cannot individually provide Canadian clearing account numbering or Payment Canada settlement. An offshore EMI may offer ancillary payment processing only if it registers as a money services business with FINTRAC and complies with Alberta money-services licensing requirements. However, for DoorDash and UberEats payout rails, a Canadian-chartered-bank or ATB Financial account is operationally required because merchant settlement schedules and clearing codes in Canada are bank-account based. An EMI can serve as a supplementary disbursement/float instrument but not as the primary treasury rail for the ULC.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Attendance by directors is not statutorily mandated for every account opening, but the bank's own AML/KYC policies will govern. Most large Canadian banks permit remote identification through a secure video interview, electronic signature, and notarized or apostilled corporate documentation. A wholly remote opening is realistically possible for foreign directors if the legal entity is in good standing, the beneficial-ownership register is transparent, and the relationship manager accepts the corporate KYC pack. In practice, banks may require at least one director, officer, or authorized signatory to attend an Alberta branch for an original signature verification, particularly when the ULC has non-resident unlimited-liability shareholders or complex ownership. To eliminate friction, the dossier should include Arthur? An Alberta-licensed corporate/commercial lawyer should provide a confirmation letter and should attend or arrange the interview as legal counsel to the ULC.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Delivery-only ghost kitchen without traditional storefront presence or regular foot-traffic receipts
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Alberta Health Services food-handling permit; commercial kitchen lease or sublease; equipment invoices or lease schedules; gas and electrical inspection certificates; municipal business licence; DoorDash and UberEats partner agreements; monthly payout statements; kitchen production schedule; staffing rosters; and a written operational narrative establishing the physical kitchen facility as a real revenue-generating asset.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident ownership and unlimited-liability corporate structure causing uncertainty regarding ultimate beneficial owner and tax classification
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified certificate of incorporation and constituent declaration for the Alberta ULC; extract from Alberta Corporate Registry; articles of incorporation and unanimous shareholder agreement; fully completed beneficial-ownership register; board resolutions authorizing bank signatories; passport and proof-of-address documents for all directors and beneficial owners; financial statements or opening balance sheet; and a legal opinion from Canadian counsel confirming the officers, directors, shareholders, and the unlimited-liability characteristics of the ULC.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large cross-border capital injection into a newly opened ULC account from a foreign parent or shareholder account
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed share subscription or shareholder loan agreement; source-of-wealth statement for the funding shareholder; bank reference letter from the remitting institution; personal or corporate tax returns; audited or reviewed financial statements of the shareholder; SWIFT MT103 originator and beneficiary details; a corporate resolution approving the capital contribution; and a statement of purpose clearly identifying the injection as equity or shareholder loan for working capital.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Revenue commingling with delivery-platform marketplaces and recurring USD/CAD transfers to an associated foreign brand
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Platform merchant agreements identifying the ULC as payee; daily settlement reports from DoorDash and UberEats; payout reconciliation ledger matching platform settlements to operational expenses; intercompany transfer-pricing policy or documentation; invoices between virtual brand entities; and internal treasury policy governing FX conversion, notional cash pooling, and intercompany settlement.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unlimited liability structure interpreted by compliance analysts as a pass-through entity with undefined liability envelope or offshore fraud exposure
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Alberta Business Corporations Act extract on unlimited liability companies; confirmation from Alberta Corporate Registry; Canadian tax legal opinion explaining how the ULC is a domestic taxable corporation in Canada and that the unlimited liability feature is a structural exposure for reporting purposes only; shareholder indemnity undertakings; and a director resolution confirming that the ULC, not a foreign trust or shell, is the contracting entity for all food-delivery operations.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity or shareholder-loan capital from non-resident investors should be sent via SWIFT MT103 or a direct payment instruction in CAD, USD, or other freely convertible currency. The beneficiary must be the Alberta ULC bank account held at the chosen Canadian clearing bank. The remittance must include full originator name, address, and account number to satisfy FINTRAC electronic-funds-transfer reporting when the amount is CAD 10,000 or more. There is no Canadian exchange-control permit or central bank declaration. SWIFT field 70 should state 'ULC EQUITY INJECTION' or 'SHAREHOLDER LOAN WORKING CAPITAL'; no single statutory purpose code is prescribed for Canada. The receiving bank should be provided with the properly executed equity subscription, loan agreement, source-of-funds evidence, and board resolutions. To avoid operational flags, do not split a capital injection into multiple wires below CAD 10,000; instead evidence the entire lawful transaction and accept the bank's large-wire review process.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade disbursements for kitchen supplies, food ingredients, packaging, franchise-style royalties, or SaaS subscriptions should be cleared through SWIFT MT103 for cross-border vendors and Payments Canada's LVTS/ACSS domestic clearing rails for Canadian suppliers. For high-value imports, a commercial documentary letter of credit may be opened through a Schedule I bank trade-services desk under UCP600. USD disbursements can be sent via the correspondent banking network using a Canadian branch's U.S. domestic clearing access. CAD disbursements to a supplier in Canada may be executed by wire, direct deposit, EFT, or bank draft. When importing food or food-handling equipment, the ULC must provide the Carrier - Cargo and proof-of-entry documents to the CBSA and maintain import records for seven years. DoorDash and UberEats payouts are received through their Canadian merchant settlement partners and are credited to the ULC's CAD operating account via ACH/EFT rails; no forced conversion applies if the platform settlement is denominated in CAD but the ULC may request segregated settlement accounts for platform revenues and intercompany treasury flows.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Spot foreign-exchange contracts for immediate CAD/USD conversion, executed with a Schedule I bank or authorized dealer
Deliverable CAD/USD outright forward contracts to lock future revenues or payables from DoorDash and UberEats settlement flows
Foreign-exchange swaps between CAD and USD used to roll hedging positions or manage near-dated liquidity gaps
Cross-currency interest-rate swaps converting USD-denominated capital contributions into CAD-serviced balances where an intercompany loan is being hedged
Buy-side FX options and zero-cost collars purchased from a chartered bank to hedge adverse CAD/USD movements without limiting upside beyond the collar range

Non-deliverable forwards on exotic currencies used only for settlement risk in non-convertible supplier jurisdictions; because the Canadian dollar is fully convertible, NDFs on CAD are generally unnecessary and are permissible only where the counterparty or clearing venue cannot settle CAD deliverable forwards

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within two months after each anniversary date of incorporation or registration.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing may result in registry non-compliance and administrative dissolution. Failure to file annual returns for two consecutive years may trigger dissolution proceedings after prescribed notices.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due six months after the corporation's taxation year-end. Corporate tax balance is generally due two months after year-end, or three months for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalties generally apply where tax is owing, with additional arrears interest and instalment interest. Repeated non-compliance may cause account enforcement and reassessment.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: GST/HST Return, if registered and assigned an annual reporting period
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Generally due three months after the fiscal year-end for an annual filer; the exact deadline is stated in the CRA account and filing notice.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalties and arrears interest may apply. Persistent non-filing may result in assessments, collection action, and cancellation or involuntary closure of the GST/HST account.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T4 and applicable T4A Information Returns
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due on or before the last day of February following the calendar year to which the slips relate.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late, missing, or incorrect information returns may attract graduated penalties based on the number of slips and delay period, together with potential repeated-failure penalties.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No general size-based statutory audit threshold applies to an Alberta private ULC. An independent auditor is required if mandated by the articles, bylaws, shareholder resolution, financing terms, applicable securities law, or another statutory regime. Shareholders may generally waive or dispense with an audit where permitted by the Alberta Business Corporations Act.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian private enterprises may generally use Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE). IFRS may be adopted or required by the corporation's governance documents, lenders, investors, or applicable securities requirements.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: There is no routine annual UBO filing with the Alberta Corporate Registry. The corporation must maintain a transparency register identifying individuals with significant control, review it at least annually as a governance control, and update it within 15 days after becoming aware of a relevant change. Share transfers must be reflected promptly in the register of members and, where control changes, in the transparency register.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Securities and Share Transfers
Transparency Register of Individuals with Significant Control
Minute Book containing shareholder and director resolutions and meeting minutes
Articles, bylaws, shareholder agreements, and issued share certificates or equivalent records

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 250-800 annually for a commercial registered-office and corporate-records service; additional fees may apply for mail forwarding, nominee services, or filing support.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,000-10,000 for a small private ULC, depending on transaction volume, payroll, inventory, revenue complexity, related-party transactions, and audit scope.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined general corporate income tax rate: 15% federal plus 8% Alberta. The combined small-business rate may be 11% for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) on eligible active business income within the applicable business limit, comprising 9% federal and 2% Alberta. A non-resident-controlled ULC ordinarily cannot access the CCPC small-business rate.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: The general combined rate is 23%. Qualifying CCPCs may obtain the federal small-business deduction and Alberta small-business rate on eligible active business income, subject to the applicable business limit and associated-corporation rules. The federal immediate expensing rules, capital cost allowance, SR&ED investment tax credit, Alberta innovation and employment-related incentives, and other targeted credits may reduce taxable income or tax payable where statutory conditions are satisfied. Canada generally has no broad corporate tax holiday for a foreign-owned Alberta ULC. A ULC may be fiscally transparent or disregarded for foreign tax purposes only where the relevant foreign jurisdiction accepts that classification; Canadian income tax treatment remains subject to Canadian corporate tax rules.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, including applicable schedules, filed electronically through CRA-certified tax software using the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) corporation internet filing system, generally through My Business Account or Represent a Client. Alberta corporate income tax is administered through the CRA and the Alberta AT1 Corporation Tax Return and related schedules are filed with the T2 package. A corporation with non-resident transactions may also file Form T106, Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; corporate income tax instalments are generally monthly, or quarterly where the statutory eligibility conditions are met.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 and AT1 returns are due six months after the end of every taxation year. Any remaining balance is generally due two months after year-end, or three months after year-end for an eligible CCPC meeting the statutory conditions. Instalment deadlines arise during the year based on the corporation's prior-year tax and statutory instalment method. A corporation must file even if it has no tax payable, has no taxable income, or expects a loss.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number, corporation type, tax year start and end dates, province or territory of permanent establishment, mailing address, fiscal-period information, and principal business activity.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the exact Alberta legal name and registered office information. Report the Canadian business number and identify the Alberta permanent establishment. A foreign parent, shareholder, or ultimate owner does not replace the Canadian corporation as the T2 filer.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Related and associated corporations, ownership, control, and allocation of the business limit.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose foreign parent companies, related Canadian companies, associated corporations, and common-control relationships. Do not claim the CCPC small-business deduction unless the ULC satisfies the Canadian-control and other statutory conditions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net income for income tax purposes reconciliation, including accounting income, non-deductible expenses, non-taxable amounts, timing adjustments, and other tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile financial-statement profit from the ghost-kitchen and virtual-brand operations to Canadian taxable income. Remove non-deductible expenses and separately identify related-party charges, foreign exchange items, provisions, and expenses attributable to non-Canadian activities.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax calculation, federal and provincial tax, refundable taxes, credits, and balance payable or refund.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the applicable federal and Alberta rates to taxable income. Separate general-rate income from any qualifying small-business income and preserve supporting calculations for eligibility.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance for depreciable property, including additions, dispositions, undepreciated capital cost, and available classes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include qualifying kitchen equipment, leasehold improvements, refrigeration, production assets, and technology assets. Do not deduct accounting depreciation directly; claim capital cost allowance under the Income Tax Act.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information concerning corporations resident in Canada and non-resident corporations, including ownership, control, and relevant foreign relationships.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Complete the schedule applicable to the ULC's ownership and control profile. Document the foreign parent's tax residence, ownership percentage, directors, control rights, and any hybrid or check-the-box treatment claimed outside Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Shareholder information for shareholders owning or controlling the required percentage of voting or participating shares.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report foreign corporate and individual shareholders at the required ownership threshold and provide jurisdiction, ownership percentage, and identification details.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information concerning the corporation's income from foreign sources and foreign taxes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report foreign-source income, foreign taxes, and foreign tax credit computations where the ULC earns or receives income outside Canada. Do not use the schedule to replace Canadian withholding reporting obligations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income statement information by revenue, cost, operating expense, financing expense, and profit or loss categories.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disaggregate delivery-platform receipts, food sales, brand fees, kitchen rental or service income, commissions, refunds, chargebacks, payroll, food costs, occupancy, advertising, platform fees, and related-party charges.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: General index of financial information and financial-statement reporting information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: State whether financial statements are prepared under Canadian GAAP, IFRS, or another framework and maintain a reconciliation to Canadian tax reporting.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 300 or applicable provincial schedule
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta allocation and provincial tax information, including permanent establishments, taxable income allocation, and Alberta tax computation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income to Alberta using the applicable provincial allocation rules. A corporation operating only from Alberta will generally report Alberta taxable income, but employees, facilities, or agents in other provinces may create additional provincial filing obligations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta tax credits and incentives where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only credits supported by Alberta eligibility records, qualified expenditures, certificates, and statutory filing deadlines.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Annual information return for non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents, including goods, services, royalties, interest, management fees, loans, receivables, and other amounts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File where the statutory T106 conditions are met, including the applicable aggregate non-arm's-length non-resident transaction threshold. Report gross transaction categories, counterparties, country of residence, and transfer-pricing method. T106 reporting does not itself establish arm's-length pricing.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information return for foreign affiliates of Canadian corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File only if the Canadian ULC is a reporting entity with a foreign affiliate or otherwise meets the foreign-affiliate reporting rules. A foreign parent of the ULC does not automatically make the parent a foreign affiliate of the ULC.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign Income Verification Statement for specified foreign property exceeding the statutory reporting threshold.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Assess Canadian-resident corporate ownership of foreign bank accounts, securities, receivables, and other specified foreign property. Property used principally in an active business may be excluded, but the exclusion requires factual support.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing generally attracts a penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax plus 1% of unpaid tax for each complete month late, up to 12%, subject to statutory minimums and increased penalties for repeated or demand filings. Interest accrues on unpaid balances at the prescribed rate and may compound daily. Repeated failure, gross negligence, false statements, failure to maintain records, or failure to provide information may trigger additional penalties. Late T106 filing generally attracts CAD 25 per day, subject to the statutory maximum, with materially higher penalties for false statements or omissions. Directors may become personally liable for unremitted source deductions and certain GST/HST amounts.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on taxable dividends paid or credited by a Canadian-resident corporation to a non-resident, subject to treaty reduction. A Canada-U.S. treaty rate is generally 5% where the beneficial owner is a qualifying company holding the required voting interest and 15% in other qualifying cases. Other treaties commonly reduce dividends to 5%, 10%, or 15%, depending on ownership and treaty conditions. A dividend paid by a ULC may create additional treaty-classification and hybrid-entity risk because Canada may treat the ULC as a corporation while a foreign jurisdiction treats it as fiscally transparent.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The Canadian payer must obtain and retain a valid Form NR301, NR302, or NR303, as applicable, or equivalent reliable documentary evidence establishing the recipient's residence, beneficial ownership, treaty eligibility, entity status, and required ownership threshold. The payer must apply the correct treaty rate at the time of payment, remit Part XIII tax to the CRA by the fifteenth day of the following month, and report the payment on Form NR4 and the applicable annual information return. A certificate of residence from the foreign tax authority should be obtained where required by the treaty, payer policy, or CRA audit position. Treaty relief is not automatic and may be denied under limitation-on-benefits, principal-purpose, beneficial-ownership, anti-conduit, or principal-purpose-test provisions.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: The domestic Part XIII rate is generally 25% on royalties and interest paid or credited to non-residents, subject to statutory exemptions and treaty relief. Treaty royalty rates commonly range from 0% to 10%; treaty interest rates commonly range from 0% to 15%, frequently 10%. Ordinary arm's-length interest paid by a Canadian resident to an arm's-length non-resident is generally exempt from Canadian withholding under the statutory withholding rules, subject to exclusions such as participating debt interest, certain related-party arrangements, and other prescribed categories. Royalties for intellectual property, software rights, trademarks, brand use, know-how, franchise rights, and similar rights require classification analysis. Management or technical service fees may be subject to withholding depending on their legal characterization, treaty business-profits rules, Canadian services performed, and permanent-establishment facts.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canada has no general monetary threshold below which contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation is automatically unnecessary. Section 247 of the Income Tax Act requires arm's-length pricing and contemporaneous documentation for non-arm's-length cross-border transactions. Form T106 generally applies where the statutory aggregate non-arm's-length non-resident transaction threshold is exceeded; the commonly applicable threshold is CAD 1,000,000, subject to the detailed statutory rules and exclusions. Country-by-country reporting generally applies to a Canadian-resident ultimate parent or surrogate parent of an MNE group with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the preceding fiscal year. Canada does not impose a universal OECD-style Local File/Master File filing threshold for every Canadian corporation, but CRA may require supporting documentation and may impose penalties for inadequate documentation.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not have a standalone regime formally called Economic Substance Regulations equivalent to certain offshore jurisdictions. Economic substance remains material under the Income Tax Act's general anti-avoidance rule, sham and simulation principles, treaty anti-abuse provisions, principal-purpose tests, beneficial-ownership analysis, transfer-pricing rules, residence and central-management analysis, and permanent-establishment rules. A ULC should maintain real Canadian decision-making, commercial functions, personnel or outsourced operational capability, Alberta premises or operational access, books and records, banking controls, contracts, pricing authority, food-safety compliance, platform relationships, and evidence that the entity independently bears and controls relevant risks. A conduit ULC receiving funds and paying them immediately to a foreign owner without commercial functions is a high-risk arrangement.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Tax Reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Concealing delivery-platform revenue, cash sales, brand income, related-party payments, foreign accounts, or beneficial ownership; claiming personal expenses as business costs; fabricating invoices; or knowingly filing materially false T2, T106, GST/HST, payroll, or information returns.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Income Tax Act, conviction may result in a fine generally ranging from 50% to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded, imprisonment for up to two years, or both, in addition to reassessment, interest, civil penalties, and collection costs. Conduct involving fraud may also be prosecuted under the Criminal Code, with substantially more severe imprisonment exposure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face criminal prosecution where they directed, authorized, acquiesced in, or participated in the conduct. Directors may be assessed personally for unremitted source deductions and certain GST/HST liabilities under statutory director-liability provisions. Corporate separateness generally protects directors from ordinary corporate tax debt, but does not protect against statutory assessments, personal participation, fraud, breach of trust, or criminal conduct. Civil restitution and asset recovery may follow; travel restrictions may arise through criminal process or bail conditions, but are not an automatic tax penalty.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Unreported Related-Party Transactions and Transfer-Pricing Misstatement
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging excessive management fees, royalties, interest, brand fees, kitchen rent, procurement charges, or platform-related allocations to shift Alberta profit to a foreign affiliate; failing to maintain contemporaneous documentation; or reporting incomplete T106 data.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may reassess under section 247, impose transfer-pricing adjustments, deny deductions, assess Part XIII withholding, and apply a transfer-pricing penalty generally equal to 10% of the applicable adjustment where the statutory conditions are met. Interest and other information-return penalties may also apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face personal exposure for knowingly approving false records, source-deduction failures, or fraudulent arrangements. Ordinary transfer-pricing reassessment is generally assessed against the corporation, but director liability can arise under statutory derivative-liability provisions or through civil and criminal participation.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Improper Treaty Relief and Beneficial-Ownership Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Applying reduced dividend, interest, or royalty withholding without verifying residence, beneficial ownership, limitation-on-benefits requirements, ownership thresholds, or the tax classification of the ULC and recipient.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The payer may be assessed for the unwithheld Part XIII tax, interest, failure-to-withhold penalties, failure-to-remit penalties, and information-return penalties. Treaty benefits may be denied under anti-conduit, principal-purpose, beneficial-ownership, or other anti-abuse provisions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Responsible directors and officers may incur personal exposure for unremitted source deductions where the statutory due-diligence and director-liability tests are met. Intentional misuse of treaty documentation may support civil penalties or criminal tax allegations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company, Artificial Residency, or Conduit Arrangement
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining an Alberta ULC with no genuine commercial operations, no meaningful Canadian decision-making, nominee management, circular funding, immediate upstreaming of receipts, fabricated Alberta expenses, or contractual arrangements designed solely to obtain treaty benefits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may deny deductions, recharacterize transactions, apply the general anti-avoidance rule, deny treaty benefits, assess withholding tax, and reassess tax for applicable periods with interest and penalties. Sham transactions and fraudulent records may lead to prosecution under the Income Tax Act or Criminal Code.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face civil claims, personal assessments for statutory remittances, director-and-officer liability for knowing participation, asset seizure or forfeiture in criminal proceedings, and imprisonment where fraud or evasion is proven. A travel ban is not an automatic corporate-tax sanction but may be imposed by a court as a criminal-process condition.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register for GST/HST when required, misclassifying employees as contractors, omitting Uber Eats or DoorDash settlement income, failing to remit source deductions, or treating platform commissions and refunds inconsistently.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation may face GST/HST reassessments, net-tax and source-deduction interest, late-filing and late-remittance penalties, gross-negligence penalties, and denial of input tax credits where invoices or records are deficient.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally assessed for unremitted payroll source deductions and certain GST/HST amounts. Personal exposure can continue after dissolution or insolvency, subject to statutory limitation periods and due-diligence defenses.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Corporate Records, Beneficial Ownership, and Annual Return Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to maintain Alberta corporate records, registered-office information, shareholder and beneficial-ownership records, minute books, accounting records, or required annual corporate filings; using nominees to obscure ownership.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Alberta corporate registry may impose late fees, administrative dissolution, restoration costs, and compliance orders. Tax authorities may impose record-keeping and information penalties and draw adverse inferences from missing records.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face statutory offences, fines, disqualification consequences, civil claims, and personal exposure where inaccurate records conceal tax evasion, creditor prejudice, or unlawful distributions. Dissolution does not eliminate tax debts or director-liability assessments.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Accepting criminal proceeds, structuring cash deposits, disguising beneficial ownership, using nominee shareholders, laundering platform receipts, or knowingly assisting criminal clients or counterparties. A normal restaurant or ghost-kitchen operator is not automatically a FINTRAC reporting entity solely because it receives electronic platform payouts, but obligations may arise if the business conducts a regulated financial activity or falls within another listed reporting sector.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Proceeds-of-crime and money-laundering offences may result in substantial fines, forfeiture, and imprisonment under the Criminal Code and Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act. Regulated reporting entities may face administrative monetary penalties for registration, suspicious-transaction, record-keeping, or compliance-program failures.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, officers, beneficial owners, and employees who knowingly participate may face criminal charges, imprisonment, forfeiture, restitution, asset restraint, and court-imposed travel restrictions. Corporate liability does not shield individuals who personally commit or authorize laundering conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Distributing profits to foreign owners while insolvent, without adequate corporate solvency, without accounting for tax liabilities, or while disguising distributions as deductible royalties, loans, management fees, or expense reimbursements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The distribution may be voidable under applicable Alberta corporate law, recharacterized for tax purposes, treated as a shareholder benefit or dividend, and subject to withholding tax, interest, penalties, creditor remedies, and insolvency clawback.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who authorize prohibited distributions may face restitution claims, contribution claims, creditor actions, disqualification, and personal liability under corporate statutes. Personal liability is distinct from ordinary shareholder liability and may arise where directors breached statutory solvency duties or acted fraudulently.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Food, Employment, and Licensing Non-Compliance with Tax Consequences
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a delivery-only kitchen without required municipal, Alberta health, food-safety, business, employment, or premises approvals; paying workers off-book; or using unlicensed subcontractors and suppliers.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Authorities may issue inspection orders, administrative penalties, licence suspension, closure orders, employment assessments, payroll reassessments, and prosecution for serious violations. Unlawful payments may be denied as deductions or treated as unreported employment income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may be personally prosecuted for offences involving unsafe food, workplace violations, or knowing payroll and tax evasion. Civil restitution, compensation orders, and travel restrictions may follow criminal proceedings; imprisonment depends on the governing statute and facts.
